conservation.help_by: Give wildlife space; pick reef-safe sunscreen and careful finning.
conservation.caution_against: Don’t feed fish, chase animals, or pocket living souvenirs.

life_info.eating: Fish ambushed with a burst of speed. Hangs motionless, then rockets forward.
life_info.habitat: Reef edges, seagrass, and nearshore blue water — still as a spear. Young school; big adults often hunt alone.

fun_facts: Usually ignore people — shiny jewelry interests them more than you do.
Teeth point backward: once a fish is in, it’s not swimming out.

conservation.help_by: Leave living plants where they grow; reduce nutrient runoff when you can.
conservation.caution_against: Don’t uproot algae or seagrass for aquariums without permits.

life_info.eating: Photosynthetic primary producer. Makes energy from sunlight (and sometimes from clear shallow water light).
life_info.mating: Spreads by spores, seeds, propagules, or creeping rhizomes depending on the species.
life_info.habitat: Sand and reef flats; feather-like fronds from runners. Forms habitat structure that shelters fish, crabs, and invertebrates.

fun_facts: Feathery fronds sprout from a creeping stolon like underground stems.
Related species can be invasive outside their home range.

conservation.help_by: Give wildlife space; pick reef-safe sunscreen and careful finning.
conservation.caution_against: Don’t feed fish, chase animals, or pocket living souvenirs.

life_info.eating: Fish, crabs, and octopus hunted at night. Ambush from a crevice; pharyngeal jaws pull prey in.
life_info.mating: Open-water larval stage before settling on a reef.
life_info.habitat: Reef holes and wrecks; head often peeking from a den. Looks angry when breathing — open mouth is gill work.

fun_facts: The green color is a mucus coat over brownish skin.
Give dens space; a surprised moray has a strong bite.

conservation.help_by: Keep nesting beaches dark and clear; support marine protected areas.
conservation.caution_against: Never buy turtle products; don’t block crawlways or touch nesting turtles.

life_info.eating: Adults prefer seagrass and algae (they are mostly vegetarian). Young turtles snack more widely, including jellies and small invertebrates. Grazes like a lawnmower on the seafloor, often resting between bites on sandy patches snorkelers can spot.
life_info.mating: Mates in the water near nesting beaches. Females return to lay eggs in sandy pits — hundreds of eggs, many trips per season.
life_info.habitat: Warm shallow seas — coral reefs, seagrass beds, and calm lagoons. Nests on sandy beaches; hatchlings scramble to the water at night. Usually solitary travelers, but groups gather on good grazing flats. They recognize some feeding spots across years.

fun_facts: They are not named for a green shell — the fat under the shell is greenish from all that salad.
A turtle can hold its breath for hours while napping underwater… which makes “hold still for the photo” their specialty.
